title: Podcast with Walter Raquet, Chairman and CEO of Symmatrics - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Symmatrics CEO Walter Raquet pitches a revived one-time-pad symmetric encryption system using quantum random number generators, claiming it avoids the math-based asymmetric crypto that quantum computers threaten. The product, finished in June, is in trial installs, lacks NIST certification and targets a claimed January 1, 2027 federal quantum-resistance deadline.

insights.claim: The one-time pad is regarded as perfectly secure but was dropped by intelligence agencies in the early 2000s because couriers had to carry matching key material to each party; Symmatrics aims to remove that bottleneck with electronic delivery of QRNG-generated keys.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: The thesis is that key logistics, not cryptographic strength, was the barrier, so cheap QRNGs reopen an old technology.

insights.claim: Raquet argues true random number generation at scale only became feasible with quantum random number generators in the early 2020s, which is why one-time-pad systems could not be built before.
insights.speaker: Walter Raquet
insights.so_what: Cheap QRNG hardware is the enabling component; watch QRNG vendors as a derivative play.
insights.locator: the quantum random number generators really didn’t come into play until the early 2020s

insights.claim: Symmatrics says three QRNGs costing $6,000 to $8,000 each can generate about 10 trillion keys a year, and its key distribution center can create trillions of random numbers, store billions and distribute about eight million per second.
insights.speaker: Walter Raquet
insights.so_what: Low claimed hardware cost implies margin potential if the product is accepted, but these are unverified vendor figures.
insights.locator: Walter describes a key distribution center

insights.claim: In Symmatrics' banking example each transaction is wrapped in as many one-time keys as the message needs, the bank destroys those keys and sends back a new transaction key, so no passwords or reusable credentials exist.
insights.speaker: Walter Raquet
insights.so_what: Eliminating reusable credentials targets the attack surface behind most breaches, if the key-distribution bootstrapping holds.

insights.claim: Keys move between sites over a 'quantum protected network' (QPN) built on dedicated three-foot-by-three-foot hardware boxes in each data center, which Raquet says can secure transactions, files, calls, texts and emails.
insights.speaker: Walter Raquet
insights.so_what: Hardware-box deployment means a slow, per-site sales cycle rather than a software rollout.
insights.locator: So we have what we call a QPN instead of a VPN

insights.claim: Symmatrics finished its product in June 2026 and is installing it on a trial basis at several companies, with pricing per box depending on use case and customization; it has about 20 staff plus roughly 30 engineers and is based in Tysons Corner, Virginia.
insights.speaker: Walter Raquet
insights.so_what: Early commercial stage with small headcount: execution and certification risk are high.
insights.locator: The product is in process now of being deployed

insights.claim: Raquet says the product will be focused on the US and its allies, implying export limits to other countries.
insights.speaker: Walter Raquet
insights.so_what: Allied-only availability fits a national-security positioning and limits addressable market.
insights.locator: obviously we’re focused on the US

insights.claim: Symmatrics does not yet have NIST certification and is working with NIST to obtain it ahead of what Raquet describes as a January 1, 2027 federal quantum-resistance deadline.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Certification, not technology, is the gating item for government sales; a miss would undercut the deadline pitch.
insights.locator: The company does not yet have NIST certification.

insights.claim: Raquet says Symmatrics did not fit NIST's post-quantum process because NIST was working on asymmetric algorithms, and that it only recently began engaging NIST for certification.
insights.speaker: Walter Raquet
insights.so_what: A symmetric, non-math alternative sits outside the standardized PQC path, so its acceptance is uncertain.
insights.locator: we didn’t fit into NIST’s box because they were doing all asymmetric

insights.claim: Raquet claims his is probably the only known technology that can make organizations quantum resistant by the deadline, and that it is quantum secure now and could be called 'quantum proof' once enough systems are deployed.
insights.speaker: Walter Raquet
insights.so_what: A strong promotional claim that conflicts with the NIST PQC consensus; treat as unverified.
insights.locator: we have the only probably known technology that could actually make that happen

insights.claim: Raquet says Symmatrics filed patents on one-time-pad symmetric key use, that 76 other firms later filed similar patents, and that major companies would need to license the technology.
insights.speaker: Walter Raquet
insights.so_what: Patent position is the claimed moat; the licensing claim is untested.
insights.locator: we filed the patents on the use of one-time pad symmetric keys

insights.claim: Raquet cites cybercrime of $10.5 trillion in 2025 rising to $23 trillion in 2027 (up from about $5 trillion when he joined) as evidence that asymmetric encryption is severely broken.
insights.speaker: Walter Raquet
insights.so_what: Unsourced headline numbers used as sales framing; do not treat as addressable market.
insights.locator: there was $10.5 trillion of cybercrime in 2025

insights.claim: Symmatrics is targeting adoption by Microsoft and NVIDIA and says it has met with the White House and government, hoping major-company adoption in the next year.
insights.speaker: Walter Raquet
insights.so_what: Binary catalyst: a big-tech partnership would validate the approach; none is announced.
insights.locator: Microsoft would be an ideal candidate for our technology

insights.claim: Raquet says the system could also secure central bank digital currency transactions and every app on a smart device.
insights.speaker: Walter Raquet
insights.so_what: Broad claims extend the pitch to CBDC security, a speculative adjacency.
insights.locator: With the advent of central bank digital currency
